quote.translation: As I shall discuss in detail later, Aristotle's symbebēkos (συμβεβηκός, accidens) corresponds to categorical contingency; automaton (αὐτόματον, casus) and tychē (τύχη, fortuna) correspond to hypothetical contingency; and endechomenon (ἐνδεχόμενον, contingens) corresponds to disjunctive contingency.

regions.text: なほミローはアリストラレスおよびタールノーに於ける偶然といふ論交のなかでアリストテレスの偶然論とクールフーの偶然論にあつて共通なる偶然の三方面を指摘してるる。第一は「選選」（rencontre）である。第二は「稀有」（rarcte）である。第三は「一つの可能」（mpossible）である（GastonMilhaud,EtudessurlaPensteScientifiq

quote.translation: Milhaud, in an essay on chance in Aristotle and Cournot, identifies three aspects of chance that the two theories share: first, "encounter" (rencontre); second, "rarity" (rareté); third, "a possible" (un possible) (Gaston Milhaud, Études sur la Pensée Scientifique, 1906, pp. 137-158; Revue de Métaphysique et de Morale, 1902, pp. 667-681).
Now "encounter" means the encounter of one series of grounds with another series of grounds, and so is nothing other than hypothetical contingency.

regions.text: 然るに「連選」こは一つの理由系列と他の理由系列との遭過を意味してゐるから、假脫的偶然にほかならない。また稀有をは稀れにしか所屬せぬ意味であるから、概念と微表との間に存する定言的偶然でなげればならない。

quote.translation: "Rarity", meaning what belongs to a thing only rarely, must be categorical contingency, which lies in the relation between a concept and its marks.

regions.text: また「一つの可能とは同等に可能なる幾つかの離接肢の中に於ける一つの可能を意味してゐるから、離接偶然にほかならない。

quote.translation: And "a possible", meaning one possible among several equally possible disjuncts, is nothing other than disjunctive contingency.

quote.translation: His examples of what is not lawlike are that Saturn, and not the earth, has a ring, and that Frederick the Great won the battle of Leuthen, and he is therefore pointing to the disjunctive isolation of disjunctive contingency over against the universal inclusiveness of law.
